questions.text: What is the direct purpose of seasoning lumber?

options.text: To remove moisture from the wood
To add mortar to the wood
To convert board feet to cubic yards
To classify brick bonds

questions.rationale: Seasoning is the removal of moisture from lumber.
questions.explanation: Heat and compression describe thermal modification, not pressure treatment. Forced air and submersion describe dip treatment, which is less effective than pressure treatment. Steam and soak describe kiln drying or surface treatment, not pressure treatment. Pressure treatment uses a vacuum phase (extracting air from the wood) followed by a high-pressure phase (100—200 psi) to inject preservative solution deep into the lumber. Pressure treatment is a two-phase process: vacuum + high-pressure injection. This is more effective than any single-phase method.

questions.text: Which benefit is source-safe for seasoned lumber?

options.text: Less shrinkage and warping with better nail-holding than green lumber
Guaranteed immunity from all termites
Automatic fireproofing
No need for any finish in exterior exposure

questions.rationale: The checked source lists reduced shrinkage, checking, splitting, warping, and better nail-holding as benefits of seasoned lumber.
questions.explanation: This reverses the values; air-drying does not reach 12—15% in tropical climates. 25—30% is too wet; air-dried wood does not reach this in the Philippines without standing water. 8—10% is overly dry and would be achieved only with kiln drying, not air drying. Air-drying reaches equilibrium moisture content (EMC) determined by local climate. The Philippines' high relative humidity prevents wood from drying below 18—20% without kiln treatment. Optimal building moisture is 12—15%, so kiln drying is preferred. Air drying in tropical Philippines is insufficient for optimal strength and durability; kiln drying is necessary to reach target moisture content below 15%.
questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 Section 2401 (moisture considerations); AWPA U1 treatment standards (dry lumber requirement)

questions.text: Which condition best supports fungal decay in wood?

options.text: Damp wood under favorable temperature conditions
Completely dry wood below normal decay moisture conditions
Lumber measured in board feet
A plywood sheet fastened near an edge

questions.rationale: Wood decay is tied to moisture and biological activity. Damp wood under favorable conditions is the risky condition.
questions.explanation: Borate is insufficient; copper-based preservatives are required for UC3A. UC3A does require preservative treatment in tropical climates; NSCP 2015 mandates treatment for exterior exposure. Native hardwoods are excellent for decks but must be pressure-treated or regularly finished/sealed; borate treatment is still insufficient. AWPA UC3A specifies exterior above-ground use: roof over-hangs, uncovered porches, siding. Borate is UC1 only because it leaches rapidly in wet environments. Even UC3A (not in soil contact) receives rainwater and morning dew in tropical Philippines. Copper-based pressure-treated preservative (ACQ or CA-B) is required to prevent decay and termite attack. Match preservative to use category: UC1=borate, UC3/UC4=copper-based pressure treatment. Do not mix categories; borate is never acceptable for exterior applications.
questions.code_citation: AWPA Standard U1 Use Category definitions; NSCP 2015 Section 2401.3

questions.text: Why is brush application limited as a complete preservation method?

options.text: It mainly treats the surface and does not provide the same penetration as pressure treatment
It converts lumber to masonry
It removes all moisture instantly
It is the same as kiln drying

questions.rationale: Brush treatment is a surface application; it does not match pressure-treatment penetration.

questions.text: Which statement is source-safe about kiln drying and preservation?

options.text: Kiln drying reduces moisture but is not the same as chemical pressure treatment
Kiln drying always adds preservative chemicals
Kiln drying makes wood impossible to nail
Kiln drying is a mortar-joint method

questions.rationale: Kiln drying is a moisture-reduction method. Chemical pressure treatment is a different preservation method.
questions.explanation: Brush application does not cause checking (improper drying does); this is not the structural concern. Cost is secondary to durability; code requirements mandate adequate penetration. Annual re-application is not practical for structural lumber buried in soil; deep penetration from pressure treatment is required. Decay and insects (termites, beetles) can penetrate 1/4 inch in months, reaching unprotected interior wood. Ground contact and soil contact expose the wood to constant wetness and biological attack. Only pressure treatment (achieving deep penetration of 0.5—1.5 inches or more) provides reliable long-term protection. Brush, spray, and dip treatments are surface treatments only. For ground contact and deep structural protection, pressure treatment (AWPA U1) is required.
questions.code_citation: AWPA Standard U1; NSCP 2015 Section 2401.3 (preservative-treated lumber criteria)
